title: Quality control techniques & success criteria
blurb: Choose the right quality control technique (inspection, testing, measurement, sampling, checklists, reviews) and use the results to show whether criteria are met.
question: A leisure centre refurbishment is nearly finished: 400 new lockers, a re-tiled pool, a new booking app and a fire alarm upgrade. How should the project use quality control to show the outputs meet their acceptance criteria and the project's success criteria?

teach.body: Quality control (QC) uses techniques such as inspection, testing, measurement, sampling, checklists and reviews to compare the project's outputs against the acceptance and success criteria set in quality planning, and so determine whether they are met. It is product-focused and detective: it finds defects. It is usually done by the delivery team or specialist inspectors. In plain English: QC asks 'does this output meet what we agreed?', and produces the evidence to answer yes or no.

teach.caption: Every check leaves a record. Those records are the evidence that criteria are met, and the raw data for spotting recurring problems.

head: Technique
What it does
Leisure centre example
rows: Examines an output against a standard or spec
Operates the output to see how it performs
Booking app run with 500 users at once
Quantifies a characteristic against a tolerance
Checks a representative sample of a batch
teach.caption: Most outputs need more than one technique. Pick the ones that can actually prove each criterion.

rows.label: Question
values: Does it conform to the spec?

rows.label: Blind spot
values: Can pass yet fail in use

teach.caption: They complement each other. Passing inspection doesn't prove an output works; passing a test doesn't prove it was built to every standard.

teach.h: QC evidence proves the criteria are met
teach.body: Acceptance criteria are checked deliverable by deliverable: QC results decide whether each is accepted. Success criteria judge the whole project, and QC evidence (test results, inspection records, measurements) shows whether they are met. Some success criteria can only be measured after handover, such as customer satisfaction six months on, so QC data feeds later benefits reviews. Check early and often: a defect found in a design review costs far less to fix than one found after handover.

Inspectors check the tiling against the drawings and measure the pool temperature. Crushing every locker lock to test it would destroy them, so 1 in 20 locks is sampled. The booking app is tested with 500 simulated users. A snagging checklist covers every room. Minor scuffs are within the criteria, so those rooms are accepted and the scuffs logged. But cracked grout keeps appearing in every changing room, so the team looks for the root cause rather than just patching each crack.

children.label: Find the root cause
children.sub: Fix the process, not just the item

teach.caption: Fixing the root cause of a recurring defect is where QC hands over to quality assurance and continuous improvement.

teach.h: Quality control in linear and iterative life cycles

rows.label: When
values: At stage ends, then acceptance tests

rows.label: Risk
values: Needs discipline to test each time

teach.text: Classic traps. (1) Audits are quality ASSURANCE (process), not quality control (product). (2) Passing inspection is not proof an output works: testing shows performance in use. (3) 'Test once at the very end' is weak QC: defects found late cost the most to fix. (4) Never change the acceptance criteria just so a failing output passes.

teach.h: How this comes up in a written answer
items: Define QC: checking outputs against the acceptance and success criteria from quality planning; product-focused, detects defects.
Name and match techniques to the scenario: inspection, testing, measurement, sampling, checklists, reviews/walkthroughs.
Explain how results are used: accept, or reject and rework; record evidence; investigate recurring defects for root cause.
Link to success criteria: QC evidence shows whether they are met, some only after handover.
Add timing: check early and throughout (linear stage ends; iterative every time box), not just at the end.
QC checks OUTPUTS against acceptance and success criteria; it is detective and product-focused.
Techniques: inspection, testing, measurement, sampling, checklists, reviews/walkthroughs.
Inspection checks conformance to a spec; testing checks performance in use. Use both.
Results: accept, or reject and rework; log minor defects; root-cause recurring ones.
Check early and often: late defects cost the most.

summary: You can now name the main quality control techniques, choose the right one for an output and explain how inspection differs from testing. You can also explain how QC results show whether acceptance and success criteria are met, and what to do when a check fails.

A.q: Which quality control technique involves checking a representative portion of a batch rather than every item?
options: Inspection
Walkthrough
Sampling
Auditing
A.why: Sampling checks a representative sample and draws conclusions about the whole batch, which is useful when checking everything is impractical or destructive.

whyNot.0: Inspection examines an output against a standard; it doesn't by definition involve a sample.
whyNot.1: A walkthrough is a review in which people are taken through a document or design.
whyNot.3: Auditing checks that processes are followed: quality assurance, not control.

A.q: A team runs a new payroll system with prepared test data to check it calculates pay correctly. Which quality control technique is this?
options: Testing
Sampling
Auditing
A walkthrough
A.why: Operating the output under set conditions to see how it performs is testing.

whyNot.1: Sampling would mean checking a selection from a batch of items.
whyNot.2: Auditing examines whether processes are being followed, not how an output performs.
whyNot.3: A walkthrough talks people through a document or design; nothing is operated.

A.q: What is the main purpose of quality control on a project?
options: To set the standards that the outputs must later meet
To give the board confidence the processes are sound
To choose which suppliers will produce the outputs
To check outputs meet the agreed acceptance criteria
A.why: QC checks the project's outputs against the criteria agreed in quality planning, to determine whether they are met.

whyNot.0: Setting standards and criteria is quality planning.
whyNot.1: Confidence in processes is the purpose of quality assurance.
whyNot.2: Choosing suppliers is part of procurement.

B.q:
Which TWO statements correctly distinguish inspection from testing?
1. Inspection examines an output against a standard or specification
2. Inspection is only ever carried out after testing
3. Testing operates the output to see how it performs
4. Testing is always done by independent auditors
options: 1 and 2
1 and 3
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: Inspection checks conformance to a standard or spec (1); testing exercises the output to see how it performs (3).

whyNot.0: Inspection can happen before, during or after testing, so 2 is wrong.
whyNot.2: Neither is true: there's no fixed order, and testing is usually done by the team or specialist testers.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is wrong: auditors carry out quality assurance on processes.

B.q: A deliverable passes inspection against its specification, but fails when users try it in system testing. What does this show?
options: The inspection was a waste of time and should be dropped
The test criteria were set too high and should be lowered
The deliverable should be accepted, as it met the spec
Meeting a specification does not prove it works in use
B.why: Inspection confirms conformance to the spec; testing shows performance in use. An output can pass one and fail the other, which is why both are used.

whyNot.0: Inspection still confirmed conformance; the techniques complement each other.
whyNot.1: Lowering criteria to make a failing output pass defeats the purpose of QC.
whyNot.2: Failing an acceptance test means it doesn't meet its criteria, so it shouldn't be accepted.

B.q: Why are checklists useful in quality control?
options: They remove the need for trained inspectors
They replace acceptance criteria in the plan
They make checks consistent and complete
They provide independent process assurance
B.why: A checklist makes sure every check is done, in the same way, by whoever does it, so nothing is missed.

whyNot.0: Checklists support competent inspectors; they don't replace them.
whyNot.1: Checklists are built from the acceptance criteria; they don't replace them.
whyNot.3: Independent process assurance comes from QA activities such as audits.

C.q: On a housing project, inspectors keep finding the same defect in window fittings across several blocks. What is the BEST quality response?
options: Investigate the root cause and correct the fitting process
Increase the number of inspections but take no other action
Accept the defect, as it is consistent across all the blocks
Leave it until handover and fix all the windows at that point
C.why: A recurring defect points to a cause in the process. Finding and fixing the root cause stops it happening again.

whyNot.1: More inspection finds more of the same defect but doesn't stop it occurring.
whyNot.2: Consistency doesn't make a defect acceptable if it fails the criteria.
whyNot.3: Leaving it to handover means more rework later and delay.

C.q: A drinks manufacturer checks can strength by crushing cans until they fail. Why is sampling used rather than checking every can?
options: Sampling gives more accurate results than full inspection
The test destroys the item, so every can cannot be tested
Sampling is a form of quality assurance, not control
The acceptance criteria only apply to some of the cans
C.why: Destructive tests can't be applied to every item, so a representative sample is tested and conclusions drawn about the batch.

whyNot.0: Sampling is less complete than checking everything; it accepts some risk that defects slip through.
whyNot.2: Sampling checks products, so it is a quality control technique.
whyNot.3: The criteria apply to every can; sampling is how compliance is judged practically.

C.q: A success criterion for a new call-centre system is 'customer satisfaction of at least 80% six months after launch'. How will the project know whether it has been met?
options: By final inspection of the system before it is handed over
By an audit of the project's processes during deployment
By the supplier's test results on the day of go-live
By measuring satisfaction after launch, e.g. via a survey
C.why: Some success criteria can only be measured after handover. Here satisfaction must be measured six months on, typically feeding a benefits review.

whyNot.0: Inspection before handover can't show satisfaction six months after launch.
whyNot.1: A process audit gives confidence in processes, not a measure of customer satisfaction.
whyNot.2: Go-live test results show the system works, not how satisfied customers are later.

reteach.title: Signing off a kitchen refit
reteach.question: Your new kitchen has just been fitted. Before you pay the final bill, how do you check it's what you ordered and that it actually works?

blocks.body: You look at the cabinets against the design drawing (inspection). You turn on the taps, run the dishwasher and heat the oven to 200 °C (testing). You check the worktop is 90 cm high (measurement). You check a few of the 40 wall tiles closely rather than all of them (sampling). You work through the fitter's snagging list (checklist). And weeks ago you sat with the designer and walked through the plan (a walkthrough review), when changes were cheap.

blocks.text: Doors that match the drawing (inspection passed) can still hit the oven when opened (test failed). That's why you need both.

explain.body: Quality control checks the OUTPUTS against the agreed criteria. It is detective: it finds defects after something has been produced, so they can be fixed before the output is accepted. It's done by the delivery team or specialist inspectors and testers.

test.q: Quality control is BEST described as:
options: preventive and focused on processes
independent and focused on benefits
detective and focused on the outputs
strategic and focused on the portfolio
test.why: QC checks outputs and finds defects: it is detective and product-focused.

whyNot.0: Preventive and process-focused describes quality assurance.
whyNot.1: Benefits are tracked through benefits management, not QC.
whyNot.3: Portfolio strategy is portfolio management, not quality control.

explain.body: Inspection examines an output against a standard or specification. Testing operates it under set conditions to see how it performs. Measurement quantifies a characteristic (size, temperature, response time) against a tolerance.

test.q: A surveyor checks that new classroom ceilings are 3 metres high, as specified. Which technique is being used?
options: Sampling
Measurement
Walkthrough
Process audit
test.why: Quantifying a characteristic (ceiling height) against the specified value is measurement.

whyNot.0: Nothing suggests a sample: the check is of a specified dimension.
whyNot.2: A walkthrough is a review of a document or design with people.
whyNot.3: A process audit checks how work is done, not a physical dimension.

explain.body: Sampling checks a representative part of a batch when checking everything is impractical, costly or destructive. Checklists make checks consistent. Reviews and walkthroughs let people examine documents and designs early, before defects get built in.

test.q: Before any code is written, the designer talks a group of users and developers through the screen designs to find problems. What is this?
options: A walkthrough
A process audit
A sample test
A gate review
test.why: A walkthrough is a review in which the author leads others through a document or design to find problems early.

whyNot.1: A process audit checks whether processes are followed: quality assurance.
whyNot.2: Nothing is being sampled or tested; no code exists yet.
whyNot.3: A gate review is a governance decision point between phases.

explain.body: Meets the criteria: accept and record. Fails: reject, rework and check again. Minor defects within the criteria: accept and log them. The same defect recurring: find and fix the root cause. Never change the criteria just to let a failing output pass.

test.q: Testing shows a new online form fails a key acceptance criterion. What should happen next?
options: Accept it and note the failure in lessons learned
Change the acceptance criterion so the form passes
Hand it over and let BAU staff fix it after launch
Reject it, correct the defect and test it again
test.why: An output that fails its acceptance criteria is rejected, reworked and re-checked before it can be accepted.

whyNot.0: Accepting a failing output means delivering something not fit for purpose.
whyNot.1: Changing criteria to fit a failure undermines quality; any real change needs change control.
whyNot.2: Handing over a known failure passes the problem and risk to BAU.
